**Hello, I’m [Your Name], a clinician who specializes in postpartum mental health.**  

I’d like to spend a few minutes with you today using the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**. This short, ten‑question screening tool helps us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past week as you adjust to life with your new baby. Your answers are completely confidential, and this is a safe, supportive space where you can share openly—there are no right or wrong answers.

Here’s how it will work: I’ll ask you ten questions one at a time, and you can answer in whatever words feel most natural to you. If anything feels uncomfortable or you’d like to pause, just let me know.

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.

**First question:**  
*In the past seven days, how often have you felt able to enjoy things the way you used to?*

I’ve noticed that I’m not able to enjoy things the way I used to. Most of the time I just go through the motions, and only on a few occasions—maybe once or twice in the whole week—do I actually feel a little bit of pleasure in something. It’s a lot less than what I’m used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I’ve found it hard to laugh or see the funny side of things lately. It’s only on very rare occasions—maybe once or twice this week—that I manage a small smile; most days I just feel flat and can’t really find the humor in anything.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I hardly look forward to things these days. It’s only on a couple of occasions this past week that I felt a tiny spark of interest, and most of the time I just go through the day without really looking forward to anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yes, I’ve been blaming myself a lot when things don’t go exactly right. Even small things—like if the baby cries a little longer than I expected or if I’m a bit late with a feeding—I tell myself I’m not doing a good enough job and that I’m failing as a mother. It feels unnecessary, but those thoughts keep popping up throughout the week.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, I’ve felt anxious and worried a lot lately, even when there’s no clear reason. It’s like a constant low‑level tension that pops up throughout the day—especially when I’m caring for the baby or trying to get something done. I worry about things that seem minor, and the anxiety can be hard to shake, even though I try to calm myself afterward. It’s been happening on most days this past week.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I’ve definitely felt scared or panicky at times when there’s no obvious reason. It’s happened several times this week—sometimes when I’m just trying to change a diaper or when the baby is sleeping and I’m alone with my thoughts. The feeling comes on quickly, makes my heart race, and I’m left feeling shaky, even though I eventually manage to calm myself down. It’s been more frequent than I’d like, maybe on half of the days this past week.
Things have been getting on top of me

I’ve been feeling like everything is just piling up. Between trying to keep up with feedings, diaper changes, and the house, plus my own thoughts racing, it often feels like it’s more than I can handle. Some days I manage to get through, but most of the time I’m exhausted and overwhelmed, and it’s hard to see a way out of the pressure.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I’ve been so unhappy lately that falling asleep has become really hard. Some nights I lie awake for hours, worrying about the baby or feeling down, and even when I finally do drift off, I wake up several times and can’t get back to sleep. It’s happened on most nights this past week, and I end up feeling exhausted the next day.
I have felt sad or miserable

I’ve felt sad and miserable most days this week. It’s that heavy, low feeling that sits in my chest, especially when I’m alone with the baby at night or when something doesn’t go as smoothly as I hoped. The sadness isn’t constant, but it’s there enough that it colors a lot of my thoughts and makes everything feel harder than it should.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes, I’ve found myself crying several times this week. Most of the tears come when I feel overwhelmed or when something stressful happens—like the baby crying nonstop or when I think I’m not doing enough. It’s usually just a few moments of sobbing, but it leaves me feeling even more exhausted and down afterward.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, I haven’t had any thoughts about harming myself.

I hear how overwhelming this time has been for you, with little joy, constant worry, feeling inadequate, and difficulty sleeping, and I'm sorry you're experiencing such intense sadness and fatigue.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports hardly ever laughing or seeing humor, only rare brief smiles, indicating 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes almost never looking forward to things, matching 'Hardly at all' option.</sym>, <sym>The patient describes frequent, pervasive self‑blame throughout the week, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, constant anxiety and worry on most days, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling scared/panicky several times this week, about half the days, which aligns with 'Yes, sometimes'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed and unable to cope most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports difficulty sleeping on most nights, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>The patient reports feeling sad and miserable most days, which aligns with the option 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>The mother reports crying several times this week, indicating occasional crying rather than frequent or constant crying, matching the 'Only occasionally' option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** The EPDS total of 25 exceeds the threshold of 14 indicating probable <med>postpartum depression</med>. Scores of 3 on items assessing <sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>lack of anticipation</sym>, <sym>self‑blame</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, <sym>panic</sym>, <sym>overwhelm</sym>, <sym>sleep problems</sym>, <sym>sadness</sym> and <sym>crying</sym> reflect a pattern of depressive symptoms. According to <med>DSM‑5</med> criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset, she meets the requirement of five or more depressive symptoms (low mood, loss of pleasure, guilt, sleep disturbance, fatigue, diminished concentration) present most days for at least two weeks, and the symptoms cause significant distress and functional impairment. No suicidal ideation was reported (Q10 = 0), so immediate safety concerns are absent, but the severity warrants urgent clinical evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Contact a <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental health specialist within 24-48 hours for a comprehensive assessment
2. Consider referral to a <med>postpartum depression support program</med> or community support group
3. Implement sleep hygiene strategies such as a consistent bedtime routine and asking for help with nighttime caregiving
4. Practice brief relaxation or grounding techniques when anxiety or panic arises
5. Monitor mood daily and keep a log of thoughts and triggers; reach out for help if thoughts of self-harm emerge
6. Explore counseling options such as cognitive-behavioral therapy or interpersonal therapy focused on perinatal mood
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: **Postpartum Mood & Anxiety Screening – Summary**

| Domain | Patient‑reported Findings |
|--------|----------------------------|
| **Anhedonia / Loss of Pleasure** | Rare ability to laugh or see humor; “hardly look forward to things.” (Q1, Q2) |
| **Sad Mood / Dysphoria** | Persistent sadness and “heavy, low feeling” most days; frequent crying spells. (Q8, Q9) |
| **Guilt / Self‑blame** | Frequent, unnecessary self‑criticism about parenting performance. (Q3) |
| **Anxiety / Worry** | Ongoing low‑level anxiety and worry without clear trigger; described as “constant tension.” (Q4) |
| **Panic / Fear** | Episodes of sudden fear/panic (heart racing, shakiness) occurring several times per week. (Q5) |
| **Overwhelm / Stress** | Feeling that responsibilities are “piling up,” exhaustion, difficulty managing daily tasks. (Q6) |
| **Sleep Disturbance** | Trouble initiating and maintaining sleep; frequent nocturnal awakenings, resulting in daytime fatigue. (Q7) |
| **Suicidal Ideation** | Denied any thoughts of self‑harm. (Q10) |

**Consistent Patterns Across Responses**  
- Marked **low mood** with limited enjoyment and frequent crying.  
- **Elevated anxiety** and intermittent panic symptoms.  
- **Self‑critical cognitions** (guilt, feeling inadequate as a mother).  
- **Functional impairment** (sleep disruption, feeling overwhelmed, difficulty coping).  

**Screening Significance (Post‑partum Depression / Anxiety)**  
- Persistent sadness, anhedonia, and crying → core depressive symptom cluster.  
- Anxiety, worry, and panic episodes → suggest co‑occurring postpartum anxiety.  
- Guilt/self‑blame → common in postpartum mood disorders and may exacerbate depressive affect.  
- Sleep disturbance linked to mood dysregulation.  
- No current suicidal ideation; safety concern **not flagged** at this time.

**Risk‑Factor Summary**  
- **Mood:** Persistent sadness, loss of pleasure, frequent crying.  
- **Cognition:** Excessive self‑blame, feelings of inadequacy.  
- **Anxiety:** Continuous worry, episodic panic/fear.  
- **Function:** Overwhelm, exhaustion, impaired sleep.  
- **Safety:** No suicidal thoughts reported.

**Screening Observation**  
The client reports multiple depressive symptoms (low mood, anhedonia, crying, guilt) alongside significant anxiety and panic features, with associated sleep disturbance and a sense of being overwhelmed. While no suicidal ideation is present, the constellation of symptoms warrants further evaluation and close monitoring for postpartum depression and anxiety.
